# Sharp hyperplane concentration from sampled superlevels

This is an auxiliary volume and concentration theorem. It does not resolve
the allocation of mass across arbitrarily many coarse integer fibers.

Let L be a full-rank lattice in R^r, r>=1, of covolume v, and let a+L
be a coset. Let f:R^r->[0,infinity) be a bounded measurable function
with compact support, all of whose positive superlevel sets are convex.
Put

    T=sum_(p in a+L) f(p),       M=integral f(u) du.

The sum has finitely many nonzero terms. If T>0, there is an affine
hyperplane E spanned by r affinely independent points of a+L such that

    sum_(p not in E) f(p) <= r! M/v.                    (1)

If the positive sampled support has affine rank less than r, E may
instead be any lattice hyperplane containing its affine hull, and the
left side is zero. Thus always

    sum_(p in E) f(p) >= (T-r! M/v)_+.                  (2)

The coefficient r! is sharp even when f is a section-volume function
of a full-dimensional convex body with all its sampled fibers positive.

## 1. A finite lattice-point volume bound

If A is a finite subset of a+L spanning R^r, then

    vol_r(conv A) >= (|A|-r) v/r!.                     (3)

Triangulate conv A using every member of A as a vertex. Such a
triangulation exists: start with a triangulation of its vertex set and
insert the remaining points one at a time by subdividing all simplices
containing the inserted point in a face. Each full-dimensional simplex
has volume at least v/r!, since its edge determinant in a lattice basis
is a nonzero integer.

If the triangulation has t full-dimensional simplices, then |A|<=r+t.
Indeed its full-dimensional dual graph is connected. To see this,
connect interior points of two simplices by a polygonal path in the
interior of the convex polytope, perturbing the path to avoid all faces
of codimension at least two and to cross facets transversely. Its
successive simplices give a dual-graph path. A spanning-tree order of
the t simplices starts with r+1 vertices and adds at most one vertex
with each successive simplex, because it shares a facet with an
earlier simplex. Every triangulation vertex belongs to a full simplex.
Consequently |A|<=r+1+(t-1)=r+t. Summing their volumes proves (3).

## 2. A greedy hyperplane and one common threshold

Suppose the positive sampled support P spans R^r. Order its members
by nonincreasing f-value, with any fixed rule for ties. Select the first
point and then repeatedly the first point outside the affine span of
those already selected, until r points p_1,...,p_r have been selected.
Let E=aff{p_1,...,p_r}, and put

    b=max{f(p):p in P\E}>0.

Every selected p_i has f(p_i)>=b. In fact any point outside the final
E was outside every earlier selected affine span, so would have been
eligible whenever the greedy rule selected p_i.

For each 0<t<b define A_t={p in P:f(p)>t}. This set contains all
selected points and a point outside E of value b, so it spans R^r.
Its convex hull lies in {f>t}, by the superlevel hypothesis. Equation
(3), followed by layer-cake integration, gives

    M >= integral_0^b vol_r(conv A_t) dt
      >= (v/r!) integral_0^b (|A_t|-r) dt
       = (v/r!) [sum_(p in P) min(f(p),b)-r b].          (4)

The selected r points contribute r b to the last sum. Every point
outside E has value at most b, hence contributes its entire value.
All the other contributions are nonnegative. Formula (4) therefore
proves (1). It also proves the sharper threshold-dependent bound (4).
Strict superlevels avoid endpoint conventions; the finite identity
integral_0^b 1_{f(p)>t}dt=min(f(p),b) includes all ties exactly.

If P has affine rank less than r, a lattice hyperplane containing P
exists. In lattice coordinates the span of its integer difference
vectors is rational and has a nonzero integral annihilator; its affine
translate through any p in P is such a hyperplane. Its outside mass
is zero. This completes the theorem.

## 3. Convex-body section volumes and sharpness

Let Q be a compact convex subset of R^r_u times R^s_x, s>=1, and put

    f(u)=vol_s(Q_u),       M=vol_(r+s)(Q).

Fubini gives the displayed M. The function is bounded with compact
support and is upper semicontinuous: any Hausdorff limit of bounded
sections is contained in the limiting section, and volume is continuous
on compact convex sets, including degenerate limits. Brunn--Minkowski
gives convex positive superlevels (equivalently, f^(1/s) is concave
on its positive support). The theorem therefore applies, whether or
not Q has positive ambient volume. It also applies to Q intersected
with any closed halfspace. This last assertion supplies a possibly
different hyperplane E for each cut; no common E is claimed.

For s=0 one may instead take f=1_Q for a compact convex Q in R^r.
It has the required superlevels and the same theorem holds for
counting measure T. No root f^(1/0) is used.

To prove sharpness for every r and s>=1, let Delta be a unimodular
r-simplex for L and let K be any s-dimensional convex body of volume
V>0. Set Q=Delta times K. Its sampled bases are exactly the r+1
vertices of Delta, each with section volume V. Thus M=v V/r!,
T=(r+1)V, and every hyperplane misses at least one vertex. The smallest
possible outside mass is V=r! M/v. All these fibers are positive,
and Q is a full-dimensional convex body. For s=0 use Q=Delta.

## 4. Exact retained-source reduction

For s>=1 and positive sampled mass, retain precisely the positive
sampled fibers over E. If their base affine hull is E' of dimension
r'<=r-1, let Q_E be the convex hull of those entire fibers, inside
E' times R^s. It is compact and full-dimensional in that relative
ambient space. Its lattice fibers are exactly the retained original
fibers. Indeed convexity gives Q_E subset Q; a sampled point of
conv(P intersect E) has a full-dimensional Minkowski combination of
positive source fibers, so was itself a positive sampled base in E;
and its entire original fiber was included among the generators.

The affine lattice (a+L) intersect E' is a saturated lattice of rank
r' in E', after translating by one of its points. Choose a lattice
basis of its difference lattice to identify it with Z^(r'). This
changes only base coordinates, leaves the x coordinates unchanged,
and preserves all section s-volumes and all ambient halfspace
restrictions. The retained source is therefore an actual mixed-integer
convex source with r' integer variables and s continuous variables.

For every candidate in the retained source its unnormalized depth in
the original source is at least its retained unnormalized depth: each
containing closed ambient halfspace has at least the retained mass.
The correspondence just described includes oblique halfspaces and
restrictions that are the whole relative ambient space. Consequently,
if OC is available in the smaller integer ranks 0,...,r-1, then the
original source has maximum depth at least

    (Gamma_s/2^(r-1)) (1-r! M/(v T))_+.                (5)

No smaller-rank OC is proved here. For r=1 this implication uses only
the ordinary continuous Grunbaum theorem and the retained fiber is
one actual largest-volume fiber.

## 5. Several coarse levels: an explicit bounded-level consequence

Suppose a bounded convex source has J nonempty coarse integer levels
z, each with a fine lattice coset of the same covolume v in R^r, and
s>=1 continuous coordinates. Write T_z for the fine section-volume
sum, M_z for ordinary (r+s)-volume at that coarse level, T=sum T_z>0,
and M=sum M_z. Choose E_z by the theorem in every level with positive
T_z. Their retained fine mass is at least

    sum_z (T_z-r! M_z/v)_+ >= T-r! M/v.

One such level thus has retained mass at least (T-r! M/v)_+/J.
Using the exact source reduction of Section 4 at that one level,
and assuming OC for the lower fine integer ranks, gives original
normalized depth at least

    (Gamma_s/(J 2^(r-1))) (1-r! M/(vT))_+.             (6)

In particular J<=2^k and M/(vT)<=1/(2 r!) imply the exact original
target Gamma_s/2^(k+r). When r=1 this scoped conclusion is
unconditional by ordinary continuous Grunbaum. Unlike the earlier
full-rank sampled-volume criterion, the threshold is independent of
s and also handles full-rank levels by retaining a hyperplane within
them. The restrictions on J and on the volume ratio remain explicit;
arbitrary-level allocation is still missing.
